title: Monte Vista Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Monte Vista wells have a 98 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $10,900-$19,400.
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Monte Vista show a broad mix of shallow valley wells and deeper outliers. Of 2,193 wells in the Colorado DWR records, 1,598 are recorded as constructed, 1,620 report total depth, and 475 report pump yield. That gives a useful local picture, but it does not guarantee what a new well will find on a particular lot.

Monte Vista sits in a setting where alluvial and sedimentary ground can produce good wells, while permits also identify fractured-bedrock and San Luis Valley aquifers. Neighboring wells, well spacing, septic layout, access, and the intended use of the property all matter before you buy or drill.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Monte Vista?
sections.html:
The local median well depth is 98 feet. The middle half runs from 57 to 180 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site may be working in that range rather than assuming every well is close to the median. Half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 41% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

There are exceptions. The 90th percentile is 260 feet, and the deepest record reaches 3,022 feet. That extreme should not be used as a normal estimate, but it does show why a nearby permit is more useful than a countywide guess. Aquifer conditions named in the records include unnamed or fractured-bedrock, Confined San Luis Valley, and Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifers.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Monte Vista well produce?
sections.html:
Reported yields are strong overall, with a median of 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half of reported results runs from 15.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute. 81% of reporting wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 18% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reporting wells in this dataset are listed below 5 gallons per minute. That is encouraging for household planning, but yield records are not the same as guaranteed long-term supply. Pump tests, storage, pressure equipment, and the well permit’s allowed use still matter. Exempt household-use wells are subject to Colorado rules, including the general 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Is Monte Vista’s water table getting deeper?
sections.html:
Recorded static water levels are relatively shallow. The median depth to water is 18 feet, with the middle half between 8 and 27 feet. That affects drilling decisions, pump setting, trench work, and the way a contractor plans casing and grout.

The decade comparison deserves attention: the median reported water level was 9 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. This series suggests deeper measured water levels in the newer records, but only 69 wells report a static water level, so it is not a complete monitoring network. Ask for current neighboring measurements before treating the change as a property-wide trend.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Monte Vista, and how active is the area?
sections.html:
Permit history is substantial and spans decades. The records show 105 permits from the 1950s, 93 from the 1960s, 336 from the 1970s, 133 from the 1980s, 276 from the 1990s, 376 from the 2000s, 168 from the 2010s, and 137 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers named in these records are Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.) with 216 wells, Spencer, D W with 112, and Burk Drilling Inc. (Burk, Ken C.) with 102. Treat those names as permit-history context, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost near Monte Vista?
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground around Monte Vista, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the local median depth of 98 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $4,900 to $7,400. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $10,900 to $19,400. A bid can move outside that range if the site needs greater depth, difficult access, extra casing or grout, unusual trenching, treatment, or a different pump arrangement. Get the drilling price, dry-hole terms, completion work, and testing requirements in writing rather than comparing per-foot prices alone.

sections.heading: What risks should a buyer check before drilling?
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported results, but incomplete records still leave uncertainty. Only 475 wells report a pump yield, and only 69 report static water level. A dry hole or disappointing result remains possible, especially where fractured bedrock is involved. Ask a driller to review nearby permits and explain the proposed casing, grout, target aquifer, and pump test.

Water quality also needs separate testing. Mapping within about 10 miles shows 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove contamination at a parcel. Test the existing well or new source, inspect septic setbacks and replacement-area options, and confirm that the lot can support the house, driveway, well, and septic system together.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Monte Vista
sections.html:
Before closing, pull the DWR permits for the parcel and nearby properties, then compare depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer name, use, and completion details. The local use mix is 56% domestic or household, 21% stock, 25% irrigation, and 5% monitoring, so not every nearby well is a direct model for a residence.

Check properties in Center, Del Norte, Alamosa, Mosca, Alamosa East, and Hooper only as broader regional context; the closest neighboring wells remain more useful. For a building lot, confirm the permit pathway, access for a rig, electrical service, septic design, water-quality testing, and room for repairs. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Have the driller and a water-rights professional review the site before you commit.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Monte Vista, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Monte Vista is 98 feet. The middle half of wells is between 57 and 180 feet, and 50% are under 100 feet. Depth still varies by parcel: 41% are between 100 and 300 feet, the 90th percentile is 260 feet, and the deepest record is 3,022 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Monte Vista?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50-$75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 98-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $4,900-$7,400. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,900-$19,400, before unusual access or site complications.

faq.q: How much water does a Monte Vista well produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 15.0 to 50.0 gallons per minute. The records show 81% producing more than 15 gallons per minute and 18% producing 5-15 gallons per minute. These figures describe reported wells, not a guarantee for an un drilled site.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Monte Vista?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 historic mine features, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or new well for site-appropriate contaminants, and inspect the septic system and nearby land uses before relying on the water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Monte Vista?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 9 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 18 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels in newer records, but only 69 wells report static levels. Use the comparison as a reason to check current neighboring wells, not as proof of a uniform decline across Monte Vista.
